uncited: Color and Appearance Modeling extends the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation by replacing or augmenting the fixed Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients with more flexible mechanisms to represent view-dependent color, lighting, and material properties.
It solves the limitations of base 3DGS, which struggles with complex specularities, dynamic lighting variations, and transient objects in unstructured datasets.

It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Physics and Optical Modeling](15148-physics-and-optical-modeling.md) by focusing on the radiance and material representation rather than volumetric light transport equations.
All methods in this family operate on the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation, where the scene is defined by a set of $N$ 3D Gaussians $\{G_i\}_{i=1}^N$.

Each Gaussian $G_i$ is defined by its mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}_i$, covariance matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i$ (derived from rotation $\mathbf{R}_i$ and scale $\mathbf{S}_i$), opacity $\alpha_i$, and view-dependent color $\mathbf{c}_i(\omega)$.
The rendering process evaluates the Gaussian density along a ray $\mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\omega$ and integrates contributions.
The core variation across methods lies in the definition, storage, and optimization of $\mathbf{c}_i(\omega)$ and potentially $\alpha_i$, moving beyond the fixed SH coefficients used in base 3DGS.
**Post-Processing Transformation:** Applying a learned affine transformation to the rendered image based on 3D position and view embedding [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md].
**Factorized Illumination:** Separating scene lighting (via a tensor grid) from material properties (via BRDF features) to model specular effects [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md].

**Image-Conditioned Modulation:** Using an MLP and per-image embeddings to modulate Gaussian color and opacity, enabling transient object removal and appearance synthesis [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md].
**Neural Field Substitution:** Replacing per-Gaussian SH with a shared grid-based neural field to reduce parameters and improve generalization [14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md].

**Volumetric Attenuation:** Modifying the alpha-blending equation to incorporate medium properties, such as direct attenuation $B_d$ and backscatter parameters $B_\infty, B_b$, to model light transport in non-vacuum media [15148-physics-and-optical-modeling.md].
**Layout**: Ed HashEnc: 16 levels, $2^{19}$ max entries per level, 2 feature dimensions per entry, coarsest resolution 32, finest resolution 4096.
Ed MLP: 32x32x32x6 layers, Kaiming-uniform init, Sigmoid activation.

Originating from the limitations of base 3DGS in handling complex lighting and dynamic scenes, these methods evolved to incorporate neural fields, factorized illumination, and image-conditioned modulation.
They are primarily used in novel view synthesis, inverse rendering, and augmented reality applications where high-fidelity appearance and physical plausibility are required.

The claim states that the method uses multi-resolution hash grids with MLP headers to model PBR attributes (albedo, roughness, metallic) as continuous fields, avoiding learnable parameters for varying numbers of Gaussian points. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly confirms this: it states that directly modeling attributes as learnable parameters is impractical due to varying Gaussian points, so they employ multi-resolution hash grids (Ed, Es) with small MLP headers to construct attribute fields. It further specifies that albedo is generated by Ed and roughness/metallic by Es, which are functions of the center position (continuous fields).
